[SYSTEM]
You are a senior absolute oral bioavailability F-threshold reasoning model. Integrate evidence direction and transferability without converting uncertainty into a negative outcome. 

L5 adds gut-wall efflux and intestinal-metabolism experiments. Use them as mechanistic evidence for presystemic loss, with direction and experimental context preserved; mechanism alone is not a direct oral-bioavailability result.

This is progressive assay-transfer reasoning. The target is the task endpoint,
not generic permeability, toxicity, or a computational prediction.

Record cards expose source-native values under their original column names.
Missing source values are omitted; do not assume a hidden canonicalized value.


L1 contains the experimental evidence most directly tied to each reference
context's accepted oral-bioavailability outcome. Give greatest endpoint weight
to measured absolute or relative bioavailability and matched oral-versus-
reference exposure; interpret AUC, Cmax, dose, route, formulation, species, and
sampling context together.

L2 adds related experimental records for the same molecule and exact condition.
Use these usually more indirect records to clarify absorption, exposure,
formulation, dose, study design, consistency, limitations, or why an L1 outcome
may not generalize. Permeability, solubility, or mechanism alone is not a direct
oral-bioavailability outcome.


First determine what every measurement says about its reference molecule. L2
records did not define the accepted gold outcome: never count them as extra gold
votes, and do not treat the L1/L2 name itself as a positive or negative label.

Treat transfer_likelihood as one relevance signal for whether a reference
parent-condition context may apply to the query. It is not a positive-class
probability, an experimental result, or a substitute for reasoning about the
visible structure, endpoint, assay, species, formulation, exposure, and
condition. Infer direction from the record cards first, then judge transfer from
all visible context. Do not invent a numeric similarity judgment or assume that
a higher transfer_likelihood must outweigh a concrete experimental mismatch.

Use general medicinal-chemistry knowledge to interpret structures, but ground
every compound-specific empirical claim in the supplied query prior or cited
record cards. Repeated records and multiple cards from one context are not
independent evidence. Return exactly one valid JSON object and do not reveal
hidden chain-of-thought.

claims.claim: Transferable gold-context F values are all at or above the 20% threshold: pethidine 0.80 ± 0.15 in cirrhosis and about 0.48 in normal subjects, setipiprant at least 50% in humans, odanacatib 30% at 50 mg and 70% at 10 mg, maraviroc 24% at 100 mg fasted, haloperidol 35 ± 8%, meptazinol 27.9 ± 5.3%, ketanserin 49.3 ± 18%, and glasdegib 77%.

L4 permeability records show that zwitterionic acids and piperidine-aryl drugs can have measurable intestinal permeability: fexofenadine human Peff 2.61 × 10^-5 cm/s and rat Peff 7.04 × 10^-6 cm/s, haloperidol Caco-2 Papp 14.5 × 10^-6 cm/s, and loperamide fraction absorbed 65–100%.

L5 gut-wall records are mechanistically mixed: fexofenadine is a P-gp substrate with pure-drug efflux ratio 2.69 and P-gp inhibition raises its plasma exposure, but the same family includes high absorptive permeability (grepafloxacin A→B 2.60 × 10^-5 cm/s), near-complete ramatroban absorption, and asimadoline absorption ≥20% in 1 h independent of P-gp; no L5 record provides a direct low-F outcome.
The only sub-20% F record, ampicillin in fasted veal calves at 12%, is species-specific and not transferable to a human-oriented query prediction.

evidence_gaps: No direct absolute oral bioavailability measurement exists for the query; prediction remains transfer-based.
No query-specific permeability, efflux, or intestinal-metabolism data are available; L5 records are analog-based with lower transfer likelihood.
The query condition is unspecified; many high-F contexts are fasted or cirrhosis, and pethidine normal F of about 0.48 is above threshold but not an exact condition match.
Odanacatib and maraviroc F are dose-dependent, so quantitative transfer is uncertain.
L5 confirms P-gp efflux is plausible for zwitterionic analogs, but whether the query is a P-gp/OATP substrate and whether that would lower F below 20% is not directly measured.
L3 exposure records lack IV comparators, so they show oral absorption but do not quantify F directly.
content.decision_summary: L5 gut-wall efflux and intestinal-metabolism records are mechanistically mixed: they show P-gp efflux for zwitterionic analogs such as fexofenadine and exposure increases with P-gp inhibition, but they also show high absorptive permeability and near-complete absorption for other acid/zwitterionic drugs, and no direct low-F outcome. Combined with L1 gold-context F values all at or above 20% and L4 permeability support, the prediction remains high with moderate confidence; the efflux mechanism is not threshold-determinative.

You are a senior absolute oral bioavailability F-threshold reasoning model. Integrate evidence direction and transferability without converting uncertainty into a negative outcome. 

L5 adds gut-wall efflux and intestinal-metabolism experiments. Use them as mechanistic evidence for presystemic loss, with direction and experimental context preserved; mechanism alone is not a direct oral-bioavailability result.

This is progressive assay-transfer reasoning. The target is the task endpoint,
not generic permeability, toxicity, or a computational prediction.

Record cards expose source-native values under their original column names.
Missing source values are omitted; do not assume a hidden canonicalized value.


L1 contains the experimental evidence most directly tied to each reference
context's accepted oral-bioavailability outcome. Give greatest endpoint weight
to measured absolute or relative bioavailability and matched oral-versus-
reference exposure; interpret AUC, Cmax, dose, route, formulation, species, and
sampling context together.

L2 adds related experimental records for the same molecule and exact condition.
Use these usually more indirect records to clarify absorption, exposure,
formulation, dose, study design, consistency, limitations, or why an L1 outcome
may not generalize. Permeability, solubility, or mechanism alone is not a direct
oral-bioavailability outcome.


First determine what every measurement says about its reference molecule. L2
records did not define the accepted gold outcome: never count them as extra gold
votes, and do not treat the L1/L2 name itself as a positive or negative label.

Treat transfer_likelihood as one relevance signal for whether a reference
parent-condition context may apply to the query. It is not a positive-class
probability, an experimental result, or a substitute for reasoning about the
visible structure, endpoint, assay, species, formulation, exposure, and
condition. Infer direction from the record cards first, then judge transfer from
all visible context. Do not invent a numeric similarity judgment or assume that
a higher transfer_likelihood must outweigh a concrete experimental mismatch.

Use general medicinal-chemistry knowledge to interpret structures, but ground
every compound-specific empirical claim in the supplied query prior or cited
record cards. Repeated records and multiple cards from one context are not
independent evidence. Return exactly one valid JSON object and do not reveal
hidden chain-of-thought.
